references.text: Ezekiel's prophecy about God as the shepherd who seeks out his lost sheep is the background for the parable Jesus tells in Luke 15:4-7. God himself says: "I will seek out the lost and bring back the scattered" (Ezekiel 34:11-16).

The context for Jesus telling this parable is that tax collectors and sinners came to hear him, while the Pharisees and teachers of the law grumbled because he welcomed sinners and ate with them (Luke 15:1-2). The parable is Jesus' response to this criticism.

Jesus uses parables to defend his fellowship with sinners and tax collectors, reflecting his earlier statement: "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance" (Luke 5:30-32).

Matthew includes a parallel parable about the lost sheep in a different context, where Jesus emphasizes that it is not the Father's will that any of these little ones should perish (Matthew 18:12-14).
Jesus spoke to the people in parables, as described in Matthew 13:34-35. The expression "he told them this parable" shows Jesus' characteristic teaching method.

Mark confirms that Jesus "spoke the word to them in many parables, as they were able to understand it" (Mark 4:33-34). Luke 15:3 introduces a series of three parables, all about what was lost and found.
The expression "he told a parable" (εἶπεν παραβολήν) is also used in Luke 14:7, showing Luke's consistent use of this narrative device to introduce Jesus' parables.
The psalmist compares himself to a lost sheep: "I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant!" (Psalm 119:176). This image forms an important background for the following parable.

Isaiah writes: "We all, like sheep, have gone astray, each of us has turned to our own way" (Isaiah 53:6). The prophetic image of people as wandering sheep is the foundation for the parable Jesus now tells.
